solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mischief as a result of cocktail served during 1 down 22's work

indicators.note: something served during an event is placed in the middle of it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the work of a merchant banker (1 down with 22 down) is money business
read as cock's tail: the last letter of the word cock

explanation.surface: A financier's cocktail-fuelled antics at work lead to some mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cocktail' must be split as cock + tail, giving its final K, which 'served during' drops into MONEY BUSINESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkey business is an idiom for playful or underhand trickery, the same as mischief.

clue.text: Nice sea song Ken composed in pub for financier

parts.note: in Nice, France, the sea is la mer
a chant is a song

indicators.note: the pub's word is placed around the rearranged name, so it sits in it

parts.note: a bar is a pub

indicators.note: composed means put together, so the letters of the name are reordered

explanation.surface: A financier spends time in a pub where Ken has written a sea shanty set in Nice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like an adjective, but it is the French city, where the sea is la mer.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant banker works in corporate finance, a professional financier.

clue.text: Why prisoner can go free

definitions.meaning: a prisoner walks out when the accusation is dropped and no offence is formally laid
free as in costing nothing, gratis

explanation.surface: The reason a captive is released and walks out at liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both that nobody is formally accused of a crime and that something costs nothing.

clue.text: Lure partner back having ditched Romeo

indicators.note: back means the remaining letters are read from right to left
ditched means dropped, so one letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone tries to tempt a former partner home after splitting with a Romeo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having ditched' removes the final R from PARTNER, leaving PARTNE, and 'back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure someone is to tempt them into a trap, to ensnare them.

clue.text: See 1
The Financial Times note the features that make a product desirable

definitions.text: the features that make a product desirable

parts.note: the newspaper speaking of itself says 'we' or 'us'
PS is a postscript, a note added to a letter

explanation.surface: The paper notes what makes a product appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The FT printed this clue, so 'The Financial Times' is the setter's newspaper referring to itself: US.
explanation.definitionFit: USPs are unique selling points, the marketing term for qualities that make goods attractive to buyers.

clue.text: Name one provided with happy ending after depression

indicators.note: the depression word comes after the numeral

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a dent is a small depression in a surface
if means provided, on condition that

indicators.note: ending picks out the final letter of the word happy

explanation.surface: Someone is named after a gloomy spell, perhaps with a happy ending.
explanation.definitionFit: To name someone is to identify them, as a witness names a suspect.

clue.text: Completion for some broken dinghy

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A wrecked small boat marks the end of the voyage for some.
explanation.definitionFit: A completion is the conclusion or finish of something, its close.

clue.text: The other sixty vie somehow to secure actual part exchange

indicators.note: securing something means holding it inside, so the jumbled letters enclose the other piece
somehow says the letters of sixty vie are arranged in some other way
the two parts of the word actual, ACT and UAL, swap places

explanation.surface: Sixty people compete to get a good trade-in price on a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part exchange' looks like a car trade-in, but it means the two halves of a word swap places.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The other' is British euphemistic slang for sex, as in 'a bit of the other'.

clue.text: Read not so esoteric composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters are arranged anew
not means the word so is left out of the letters

explanation.surface: Read a piece of writing that is less obscure than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not so' removes S and O from ESOTERIC, leaving ETERIC, which 'composition' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: To recite is to read aloud or repeat a passage before an audience.

clue.text: Useless organ programme to finish by 9

parts.note: an app is a software programme
an end is a finish
IX is 9 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A programme listing a pointless organ recital, ending by nine.
explanation.walkthrough: '9' looks like a reference to 9 across, but it is simply the number in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: The vermiform appendix is commonly described as a vestigial organ with no function.

clue.text: Hits to hear at first by Ruby on the radio

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of each of the two words
on the radio means the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: Ruby Wax, American-born comedian well known on British television

explanation.surface: Instructions to listen first to Ruby Wax being broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwacks are hard blows, so hits as a plural noun or a verb.

clue.text: Worry when lads race them endlessly

indicators.note: each word loses its first and last letters, leaving the inner pair of each

explanation.surface: A parent frets when the boys run off to race the others.
explanation.definitionFit: A headache is figuratively a source of worry or trouble.

clue.text: Sounds like Laurel's averse

definitions.note: split as 'a verse': the a joins the wordplay and the word verse is the definition, as in a section of a poem

indicators.note: says the words are spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: Stan Laurel, of Laurel and Hardy, so Laurel's is Stan's, said together with the a lifted off the front of averse

explanation.surface: Laurel is apparently reluctant, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'averse' must be split into 'a verse': STAN'S + A said together sounds like the answer, which means verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanza is a group of lines forming a unit in a poem.

clue.text: Fail to see Velia's letter

parts.note: to miss something is to fail to see it
Velia is the setter, so Velia's means 'I have', I've

explanation.surface: The setter overlooks her own correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: A missive is a formal word for a letter or written message.

clue.text: Not far from knight without armour?

indicators.note: armour is an outer covering, so the knight loses its outside letters

explanation.surface: A knight without his armour is closer to an ordinary man.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigh is an old word for near, close to.

clue.text: Content posed in some fancy yellow tops

parts.note: a model who posed for a painter sat

indicators.note: tops means the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A model poses happily in fancy yellow tops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' is a verb here: to content someone is to please them.
explanation.definitionFit: To satisfy someone is to please them, meeting their wishes.

clue.text: What for Manuel is not mixed grill

parts.note: Manuel is the Spanish waiter in Fawlty Towers, a British TV sitcom; what in Spanish is que

indicators.note: mixed says the letters of is not are jumbled

explanation.surface: The waiter Manuel insists the dish is not a mixed grill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What' wants to be the definition, but it is Manuel's Spanish QUE; the definition is the verb 'grill'.
explanation.definitionFit: To grill someone is to interrogate them, to put searching questions to them.

clue.text: Amazing Grace finally out for publication

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of order
finally picks out the last letter of the word Grace

explanation.surface: A recording of the hymn Amazing Grace is at last released.
explanation.definitionFit: A magazine is a periodical, a regular publication.

clue.text: See 8
Suspect soup kitchen lost note — naughty!

indicators.note: suspect means dubious or doubtful, so the letters are not in their true order
lost means the letters of the word note are no longer among them

explanation.surface: A dodgy charity kitchen has lost a note from its takings.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove N, O, T and E from SOUP KITCHEN, leaving SUPKICH, and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Puckish describes mischievous behaviour, like that of Puck, the sprite in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Mineral captured by digital camera

indicators.note: the answer is held within the letters of the words, as a camera captures a picture

explanation.surface: A mineral sample was photographed with a digital camera.
explanation.definitionFit: Talc is a soft magnesium silicate rock, a mineral used in powder.

clue.text: See 1
Help out gathering material primarily used for humour

indicators.note: out means the letters of help are put out of order
primarily takes the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: Someone helps by collecting material for a comedy act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'humour' is not comedy but one of the four bodily humours of old medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlegm was one of the four bodily fluids of medieval medicine, called humours.

clue.text: Compiler doing restoration in blue

parts.note: the setter, the compiler of the puzzle, refers to herself as I

indicators.note: restoration rebuilds something, so the letters are put together afresh

explanation.surface: A setter is depressed while doing up an old building.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo is a deep blue-violet shade of colour.

clue.text: Fancy a shag? Tory leader is appalled!

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are rearranged
leader picks the first letter of the word Tory

explanation.surface: A Conservative leader is horrified at being propositioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means filled with horror or shock, appalled.

clue.text: Spiritual leader leaving out charmer

indicators.note: leader takes the first letter of the word Spiritual
out means the letters of leaving are put out of place

explanation.surface: A guru departs, leaving his followers charmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spiritual leader' looks like the definition, but it gives only S.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali, from du Maurier's Trilby, is a manipulator who holds others in his spell.

clue.text: Apple mountain

definitions.meaning: a variety of eating apple from Japan
the volcano near Tokyo, the highest peak in Japan

explanation.definitionFit: Fuji is both a Japanese apple variety and Japan's famous volcanic peak.

clue.text: Don't stop Russian president scratching bottom, look the other way!

indicators.note: means the combined letters are read in the opposite direction
scratching means removing, so the last letter of the president's name goes

parts.note: Vladimir Putin
to peek is to take a quick look

explanation.surface: Encouragement to keep scratching, while Putin's itchy rear prompts onlookers to avert their eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching bottom' drops the last N of PUTIN, giving PUTI; add PEEK and 'the other way' reverses the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Keep it up is an idiom urging someone to continue, the same as don't stop.

clue.text: Two-piece or two wheels, not quite in one

indicators.note: not quite means the word falls just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a bike has two wheels
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Choosing between a two-piece outfit or a bicycle, which almost combine into one.
explanation.definitionFit: A bikini is a two-piece swimsuit.

clue.text: Do come and try cinema playing Notting Hill?

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are in play, moved around freely

parts.note: the words as printed, but the answer has room for only one of the two Es in the whole fodder, so one is dropped here

explanation.surface: An invitation to come along to the cinema, where Notting Hill is showing.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder DO COME TRY CINEMA has fifteen letters, one E more than the answer; the setter admitted the slip. 'playing' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Notting Hill, the 1999 Hugh Grant and Julia Roberts film, is an example of this film genre, hence the question mark.
